title: Intermediation and Deal Brokerage
notes: No university in the comparator set teaches this as a module. The set texts turn out to be better provided than the syllabi, and the journal literature is unusually strong because the question of whether intermediaries add value has been tested repeatedly in adjacent markets. The guest hour pairs an intermediary with a principal, which is the week’s question in human form.
text: RE07 Global Infrastructure Investment and Management Week 5 Intermediation and Deal Brokerage Professor Helen X. H. Bao Department of Land Economy, University of Cambridge Guest session: a fund manager and a principal investor

title: What this week does
notes: If you have only fifty minutes, run A, the fee arithmetic in D, and the Hendel evidence in E. That is the whole argument in compressed form.
text: What this week does Week 4 built the transaction. This week asks who assembles it, what they are paid, and whether the payment corresponds to anything. Intermediation is the least examined part of infrastructure finance and the most expensive: on a large transaction the advisory and arranging fees run to tens of millions before a spade enters the ground. The week is built around a single question, which is what those fees buy. 2 A Why intermediaries exist 30 min B The advisers, one by one 35 min C Arranging, underwriting and syndication 35 min D Fees: what is charged and who actually pays 35 min E Does the intermediary add value 40 min F The transaction process end to end 30 min G Principal against intermediary: the guest debate 30 min

title: What you already have
notes: This is the one week where the methodological link is genuinely universal, because the key paper is an identification problem that everybody has the training to assess.
text: What you already have Where this week draws on modules you have taken, or are taking now. Nothing below is assumed: each idea is stated in full before the module is named. 3 Your programme Where it was taught What it gives this week Real Estate Finance RE02 Michaelmas lecture 4, information and market efficiency; lecture 2, space and capital markets and pricing processes. Lent lectures 6 and 7, fees and performance, liquidity and pricing. RE01 sessions 12 and 13, securitisation structures and markets. The theory of why intermediaries exist, and the fee structures of the vehicles through which most infrastructure is actually held. Planning, Growth and Regeneration PGR07 industry seminars with Buro Happold, the Cambridge Growth Company and MHCLG, and the consultancy report assessment. PGR01 Lent lecture 11, public engagement and planning conflicts. You have already met this ecosystem in person. What you were not asked is what the advisers are paid and what they add, which is this week’s question. Environmental Policy EP07 week 8, private governance of environmental problems. EP02, environmental policy under asymmetric information. EP01 Lent week 8, non-state actors in international climate law. Certifiers, verifiers and standard-setters are intermediaries selling assurance. The principal and agent problem they solve is the same one an arranger solves. The best evidence on whether brokers add value is a hedonic pricing problem with a selection issue. Ev

title: Why intermediaries exist
notes: Establish the theory before the cast list. Students who have the theory can evaluate each adviser; students who only have the cast list can only describe them.
text: Block A Why intermediaries exist Search, information asymmetry, agency, and the reasons a market does not simply clear. Indicative length 30 minutes 4

title: The question, stated so that it can be answered
notes: Frame it as a test the intermediaries have to pass, and the week acquires a spine.
text: The question, stated so that it can be answered A pension fund has capital. A government has a project. Both want the transaction to happen. Between them sit financial advisers, arrangers, legal counsel, technical consultants, insurance brokers, rating agencies and model auditors, and they collectively take a substantial share of the money raised. The naive question is why. The better question is what specific friction each of them removes, because an intermediary that removes no friction is a tax, and one that removes a large friction cheaply is worth every basis point. This block supplies four frictions, and the rest of the week checks each intermediary against them. A 5

title: Four frictions, and what each one implies
notes: The last card is the analytical instrument of the week. Write it on the board and keep coming back to it.
text: Four frictions, and what each one implies Search Counterparties do not know each other exists. Someone who knows both sides of a thin market creates value simply by matching them. Information asymmetry The seller knows more than the buyer, and cannot credibly say so. A third party with a reputation to protect can certify what the seller cannot. Verification cost The information is available but expensive to check. One specialist checking once for many parties is cheaper than each party checking separately. Agency and coordination Multiple parties must act together and each would prefer the others move first. An intermediary that assembles the group solves a coordination problem. The test For any adviser, ask which of the four it removes and whether its fee is smaller than the cost of the friction. Where the answer is neither, the fee is rent. A RE02 Michaelmas lecture 4, information and market efficiency. 6

title: The theoretical anchor
notes: The retained share as a credible signal is the key mechanism. An arranger who keeps ten per cent of a loan it arranged has skin in the game, and the participants know it.
text: The theoretical anchor 12,672 Syndicated loan deals analysed by Sufi to establish how information asymmetry shapes the structure of a lending syndicate. Sufi studies a sample covering 4,687 United States non-financial firms between 1992 and 2003 and finds a clear pattern. Where a borrower requires more intense due diligence and monitoring, the lead arranger retains a larger share of the loan and forms a more concentrated syndicate. Where information asymmetry is potentially severe, participant lenders are closer to the borrower geographically and through previous lending relationships. Reputation, of both the lead bank and the borrower, mitigates the problem without eliminating it. The reading is that syndicate structure is not administrative. It is a response to an information problem, and the arranger’s retained share is the mechanism by which it credibly says the loan is sound. A Sufi, A. (2007), The Journal of Finance 62(2), 629–668. 7

title: Certification, and why reputation is the asset
notes: This sets up the Gatti arranger certification paper precisely, and students find the argument intuitive once reputation is described as an asset with a balance sheet value.
text: Certification, and why reputation is the asset An intermediary that certifies quality is selling its reputation, which it accumulated slowly and can lose quickly. That asymmetry is what makes the certification credible: a bank that arranges a bad transaction damages a franchise worth far more than any single fee. This has a consequence students should notice. Certification value is not evenly distributed. A top-tier arranger has more reputational capital at risk and can therefore certify more credibly, which is why its involvement is worth paying for and why the market is so concentrated at the top. The empirical test of that claim is in block D. A 8

title: Relationship and transaction intermediation are different businesses
notes: The public authority as a one-off client in a repeat-player market is the theme of the week from the state’s side.
text: Relationship and transaction intermediation are different businesses A transactional intermediary is paid for a single match and moves on. A relationship intermediary invests in knowing a counterparty over years, and expects to be paid across many transactions rather than in any one. The distinction matters because it changes the incentives. A transactional intermediary maximises the current fee. A relationship intermediary will sacrifice a fee to protect the relationship, which is why the same institution behaves differently towards a repeat client and a one-off one. Public authorities are almost always one-off clients, which is the structural weakness in their advisory relationships from block B. A 9

title: Infrastructure is a thin market, and thin markets need matchers
notes: Concede the strongest version of the case first. It makes the later scepticism more credible.
text: Infrastructure is a thin market, and thin markets need matchers A market with many buyers and many sellers of a standardised good does not need an intermediary; a screen will do. Infrastructure is the opposite: each asset is unique, each transaction is large, the number of credible counterparties is small, and much of the relevant information is private. Under those conditions the search friction is severe. Somebody who knows which pension funds have appetite for a regulated asset this quarter, and which sponsor is willing to sell a minority stake, is genuinely creating value by matching them. That is the strongest single justification for intermediation in this sector and it should be conceded before the sceptical material begins. A RE02 Michaelmas lecture 2, space and capital markets and pricing processes. 10

title: Block A discussion
text: Block A discussion Seminar questions Take three intermediaries from a transaction you know and identify which of the four frictions each removes. Where you cannot identify one, what is the fee for? Sufi finds that arrangers retain more of the loan where information problems are worse. What would you expect to see in infrastructure, where the borrower has no history at all? If certification value depends on reputation at risk, what should happen to fees after an intermediary is publicly associated with a failure? A 11

title: The advisers, one by one
notes: Gatti chapter 4 is the source and it is unusually concrete. Keep asking the four-friction question of each adviser.
text: Block B The advisers, one by one Legal counsel, the independent engineer, the insurance adviser, and what each actually produces, and the second layer of intermediation the transaction cast leaves out. Indicative length 40 minutes 12

title: The cast, and what each is paid to produce
notes: The final column is the exercise. Most of the cast are verification services, which is why they are priced as professional fees. The arranger is different, which is why it is priced as a percentage.
text: The cast, and what each is paid to produce B Gatti, ch. 4; Delmon, ch. 7.5. 13 Adviser Appointed by Output Friction removed Financial adviser Sponsor or authority Structuring advice, the model, the bid strategy Verification and coordination Legal adviser Sponsors, lenders and authority separately Documents, due diligence report, legal opinions Verification and information asymmetry Independent engineer Lenders Technical due diligence, construction monitoring, completion certification Verification Insurance adviser Lenders and sponsors Cover programme, adequacy report, claims support Verification Market consultant Lenders and sponsors Demand, resource or price forecasts Verification, imperfectly Model auditor Lenders Confirmation the model does what it is said to do Verification Rating agency The issuer An opinion on credit quality Information asymmetry, at scale Arranger The borrower Committed funds, a syndicate, and certification Search, asymmetry and coordination

title: The second layer of intermediation
notes:
This is the slide that connects the week to week 3, where the same delegate list appeared as a census of the investor base and thirteen names on it were flagged as not being investors at all. Cambridge Associates, Albourne, bfinance, Aon, Redington and Lane Clark and Peacock are advising asset owners; StepStone, Pathway and Yielco are investing on their behalf.

The teaching point is that intermediation in this market runs in two directions from different parties, and the four frictions from block A apply to both. Search and information asymmetry are why an investment consultant exists at all: a mid-sized pension scheme cannot diligence forty infrastructure managers, so it buys that judgement. The agency problem is sharper here than anywhere else in the week, because the gatekeeper is paid by the asset owner but its recommendation determines the revenue of the manager it recommends, and the manager knows this.

Guard against one confusion before it happens. The cast table already contains a market consultant, who produces the traffic forecast or the price curve. That is a different job from the investment consultant here, and students who conflate them will misread the conflicts table later in this block.

The delegate list is suggestive rather than probative: it shows these firms are present in the market, not how much capital they influence. If a student asks how much, the honest answer is that the figure is not public, which is itself worth noticing about an industry that publishes league tables for everything else.
text: The second layer of intermediation Between the sponsor and the capital Everyone in the cast table: financial and legal advisers, the engineer, the model auditor, the arranger. Appointed transaction by transaction, by the sponsor, the lenders or the authority. Paid a professional fee for verification, or a percentage for placing funds. The engagement ends at financial close, or when construction monitoring ends. Their client is a party to the deal, and their output is a document that makes the deal financeable. Between the asset owner and the fund manager Investment consultants and fund-of-funds. Appointed by the investor, on a standing relationship rather than per transaction. Paid to advise on strategic allocation, to select and monitor managers, and in the fund-of-funds case to allocate at their own discretion. Not the market consultant in the row above. That one forecasts traffic, resource or price. This one forecasts nothing: it decides which managers an investor ever sees. Their client is the source of the capital, which is why a manager can be ruled out of a mandate before the sponsor has heard of it. B Delegate list for the Infrastructure Investor Forum 2026, published by PEI Group on 14 July 2026. Thirteen of the 112 attending organisations are consultants, gatekeepers or fund-of-funds rather than investors. 14

title: The legal adviser, through the stages of a deal
notes: The legal opinion is the clearest example in the module of a reputation and liability being sold as a product.
text: The legal adviser, through the stages of a deal Gatti sets out what legal counsel actually does, and the answer is not drafting. Counsel forms the sponsor group and its shareholders agreement, develops the project documents that create the revenue, negotiates the finance documents, conducts the legal due diligence and produces the report lenders rely on, delivers the legal opinions without which no lender will fund, supports the syndication, and then remains through the operating period as the contracts require maintenance. The legal opinion is worth singling out. It is a professional firm putting its own liability behind a statement that the documents do what they appear to do and are enforceable in the relevant jurisdiction. That is certification in the strict sense, and it is why an opinion from a firm with no assets would be worthless. B Gatti, ch. 4.1. 15

title: The independent engineer is the lenders’ eyes
notes: The paid-by-one, working-for-another structure is the conflict at the centre of the week. Name it here and return to it for rating agencies in block E.
text: The independent engineer is the lenders’ eyes Lenders funding a construction project cannot verify progress themselves. The independent engineer, appointed by and reporting to the lenders, conducts initial technical due diligence, monitors construction, issues progress reports on which drawdowns depend, validates mechanical completion and the provisional and final acceptance certificates, and then monitors operations. The role is a solution to a pure verification problem, and its structure is instructive: appointed by the party that needs the assurance, paid by the borrower, and required to be independent of both. That triangle appears repeatedly in this week, and it is the same triangle as a credit rating. B Gatti, ch. 4.2. 16

title: The insurance adviser, and what the cover actually does
notes: Insurance is the least glamorous chapter in Gatti and the one practitioners say is most underestimated by newcomers.
text: The insurance adviser, and what the cover actually does Advises on the programme required to make the project financeable, which is a lenders’ specification rather than a commercial choice. Produces preliminary and final reports for the construction and operating phases, on which the finance documents rely. Handles the difficult areas, which are typically business interruption after a loss, cover for delay in start-up, and the limits of environmental liability. Places bonding, including performance and advance payment bonds from the contractor. Supports claims, which is when the value of the advice is actually tested and when the adequacy of the original programme becomes apparent. B Gatti, ch. 4.3. 17

title: Advisers to the public side, and why they are different
notes: The asymmetry between a repeat player and a one-off player is the real subject here, and it is the same asymmetry as in the regulator’s problem from week 2.
text: Advisers to the public side, and why they are different An authority procuring a transaction appoints transaction advisers, usually a consortium of financial, legal and technical firms, to prepare the project, structure it, run the procurement and evaluate bids. Delmon treats their appointment and management as a topic in its own right, and for good reason. The public side is the weaker party in the advisory relationship. It transacts rarely, its advisers transact constantly, and it often lacks the capability to evaluate the advice it receives. The remedies are to appoint advisers early enough that they shape the project rather than justify it, to structure fees so that success is defined as a good transaction rather than any transaction, and to retain enough internal capability to be an intelligent client. B Delmon, ch. 7.5 and ch. 8.11. 18

title: The rating agency is an intermediary with an unusual business model
notes: Connect back to the week 3 guests. Students who heard the rating process described can now place it in an intermediation framework.
text: The rating agency is an intermediary with an unusual business model A rating agency sells an opinion on credit quality to the market and charges the issuer for producing it. That structure exists because the opinion is a public good once published: investors would free-ride on any subscription model, so the issuer pays. The conflict is obvious and has been examined at length. What sustains the model is the same thing that sustains arranger certification, namely a reputation worth more than any single fee. What weakens it is that the reputation is held across thousands of ratings while the fee is earned on each one, so the marginal incentive and the aggregate incentive point in different directions. Week 3’s guests can speak to how the tension is managed in practice. B Gatti, ch. 6.11.5.1 and ch. 8.2. 19

title: The model auditor, and why an audit of a spreadsheet is worth paying for
notes: The distinction between auditing the mechanics and validating the assumptions is the useful lesson and it transfers to any modelling work students do.
text: The model auditor, and why an audit of a spreadsheet is worth paying for A project financial model is the document from which debt is sized, ratios are calculated and the base case is agreed, and it is built under time pressure by junior analysts. The model auditor checks that the model does what its documentation says, that its logic is internally consistent, and that it correctly implements the term sheet and the tax and accounting treatment. The audit does not verify the assumptions. That is the market consultant’s job, and confusing the two is a common and expensive error. It is a pure verification service and it is cheap relative to the exposure it protects, which is why lenders require it as a condition precedent rather than leaving it to the sponsor. Week 6 builds a model. The auditor’s checklist is a good way to interrogate your own. B Gatti, appendix; Delmon, ch. 7.5. 20

title: Forecasting for a fee
notes: This is one of the sharpest connections in the module: the week 1 forecasting evidence is a statement about an intermediary’s output, and nobody treats it that way.
text: Forecasting for a fee A market consultant produces the traffic forecast, the energy yield assessment or the price curve on which the entire financing rests. It is paid by a party with an interest in the answer, its work is relied on by lenders, and it is rarely liable for being wrong. Given the week 1 evidence that demand forecasts are systematically over-optimistic, this arrangement deserves more scrutiny than it gets. The defences offered are that reputation disciplines the consultant and that lenders apply their own haircuts to the forecast. Both are partial. A haircut applied to a biased forecast is not the same as an unbiased forecast, and reputational discipline is weak where the outturn is observable only a decade later. B Flyvbjerg, Skamris Holm and Buhl (2005); Gatti, ch. 4.2.1. 21

title: Conflicts across the adviser set
notes: Every row is the same structure: the party paying is not the party relying. Ask students whether any of the mitigations actually work, and what a better design would look like.
text: Conflicts across the adviser set B Gatti, ch. 4. 22 Relationship The conflict Usual mitigation Adviser also arranges Advice on financing plan may favour the plan it will be paid to arrange Separate mandates, or disclosure and client waiver Independent engineer paid by borrower Appointed by lenders, paid by the party being monitored Direct reporting line, and reappointment controlled by lenders Market consultant paid by sponsor Relied on by lenders, engaged by the party wanting a high forecast Reliance letters, and lender-side review Rating agency paid by issuer Opinion sold to the market, fee paid by the subject Reputation, regulation, and committee process Contractor as sponsor Return earned in construction, not in operation Lenders require sponsor support and retention through completion

title: Block B discussion
notes: Question two is the most practically useful and produces good disagreement.
text: Block B discussion Seminar questions The independent engineer is appointed by lenders and paid by the borrower. Is that arrangement sound, and what would be better? An authority appoints transaction advisers whose fee is contingent on reaching financial close. What behaviour does that produce, and how would you structure it instead? Which adviser would you remove from a transaction if you had to remove one, and what would go wrong? B 23

title: Arranging, underwriting and syndication
notes: Gatti 6.1 and 6.2 are the source. This is the mechanics behind the theory in block A.
text: Block C Arranging, underwriting and syndication How a large loan is actually assembled, and what the arranger is doing that participants cannot. Indicative length 35 minutes 24

title: Advisory and arranging are different jobs
notes: The integration of the two roles in one institution is common and creates an obvious conflict, since the adviser recommending a financing plan may be the arranger who profits from it. Gatti discusses the integration explicitly.
text: Advisory and arranging are different jobs Advisory Advises the sponsor on structure, financing plan and negotiation Paid a fee for the advice, generally with a success element Does not commit capital Can be a firm with no balance sheet at all Its product is judgement Arranging Commits to provide the funds, then finds others to take most of it Paid an arranging fee expressed in basis points on the amount Commits capital, and is exposed if the syndication fails Requires a balance sheet, and a reputation Its product is certainty of funds, and certification C Gatti, ch. 6.1. 25

title: How a syndication is structured
notes: Club deals are the interesting case for this week, because they are the market’s own answer to the question of whether the arranging premium is worth paying.
text: How a syndication is structured Single-stage syndication sells down to final participants in one process, which is quicker and gives the arranger less control over the final group. Two-stage syndication brings in a small group of sub-underwriters first and then distributes more widely, which reduces the arranger’s exposure earlier. A club deal dispenses with syndication: a small group of banks that know the asset take their shares directly, with no underwriting risk and no arranging premium. Underwriting means the arranger commits the whole amount and is left holding what it cannot sell, which is why market conditions between commitment and syndication matter so much. Best efforts arranging avoids that exposure and gives the borrower no certainty, which is why it is used for weaker credits and in difficult markets. C Gatti, ch. 6.2.1. 26

title: Banks and institutional investors have learned to co-operate
notes: The scarcity framing is the useful one. Intermediation rents accrue to whoever holds the scarce factor, and in this market that alternates between balance sheet and capital.
text: Banks and institutional investors have learned to co-operate Three models have developed. In the partnership or co-investment model, an institutional investor takes a share of loans originated by a bank, using the bank’s origination capability without paying a fund’s fees. In the securitisation model, loans are pooled and tranched so that institutions can buy the rated senior exposure. In the debt fund model, a manager originates directly and institutions invest through the fund. Each is a different answer to the same problem: banks have origination capability and constrained balance sheets, while institutions have capital and no origination. Which model captures the value depends on who is scarce, and that has moved back and forth with the capital rules. C Gatti, ch. 6.2.2. 27

title: Where a bond issue puts the intermediaries
notes: This comparison is the best single exercise in block C. The same four frictions, resolved by different intermediaries with different fee structures.
text: Where a bond issue puts the intermediaries A project bond replaces a syndicate with a market, and replaces relationship monitoring with public disclosure. The cast changes accordingly: a bookrunner rather than an arranger, a rating agency doing publicly what a credit committee did privately, a trustee and paying agent holding the relationship the agent bank would have held, and a prospectus doing the work of a due diligence report. The underlying functions are unchanged. Somebody must verify, somebody must certify, somebody must coordinate the holders after issue. The bond market performs them through different institutions with different economics, and comparing the two is the cleanest way to see that the functions, rather than the institutions, are what matter. C Gatti, ch. 6.11.5 and ch. 7.3. 28

title: League tables, and what they actually measure
notes: This is a fair methodological criticism of the certification literature and worth making. Tier is a proxy, and proxies can be gamed by the parties being measured.
text: League tables, and what they actually measure Arrangers are ranked by the volume they arrange, and the rankings are published, watched and used in pitches. Position in a league table is a real commercial asset because it is the cheapest available signal of the reputation that block A said certification depends on. It is also a metric that can be managed. Volume is not quality, credit is given for roles of varying substance, and an institution that wants to rise can buy business by underwriting on thin terms. Students should treat a league table as evidence about market share and not about capability, and should notice that the studies which find certification value use tier as a proxy for reputation, which inherits the same weakness. C Gatti and others (2013). 29

title: After financial close, somebody has to run the facility
notes: A good example for the four-friction test where the answer is unambiguously favourable to the intermediary.
text: After financial close, somebody has to run the facility The agent bank administers drawdowns, calculates interest, collects and distributes payments, and holds the relationship with the borrower on behalf of the syndicate. It receives and circulates compliance certificates, monitors covenants, and convenes lenders when a waiver or amendment is required. The security trustee holds security on behalf of all secured parties, which prevents each lender from enforcing separately and destroying the asset. These roles are unglamorous, poorly paid relative to arranging, and are what makes a syndicate of twenty lenders workable as a counterparty for twenty-five years. They are also a coordination service in the block A sense, and among the clearest cases where the fee is obviously smaller than the friction removed. C Gatti, ch. 6.3.3 and ch. 7.2.3.13. 30

title: Loans trade, and that changes the relationship
notes: The transfer provision as a bargaining-power indicator is a nice practical detail for students reading a real facility agreement.
text: Loans trade, and that changes the relationship A loan sold in the secondary market moves from a lender that underwrote it to one that did not. The new holder has no relationship with the borrower, may have bought at a discount, and may have entirely different objectives in a restructuring. For project finance this matters more than for corporate lending, because a project in difficulty needs its lenders to agree a solution quickly and a fragmented, unfamiliar syndicate is far harder to assemble. Borrowers therefore negotiate transfer restrictions, and lenders resist them, and where the restriction ends up is a good indicator of which side had the stronger position at close. C Gatti, ch. 7.2.3.15. 31

title: Block C discussion
text: Block C discussion Seminar questions A borrower is offered an underwritten facility at a higher fee and a best-efforts facility at a lower one. When is the higher fee worth paying? Club deals have no arranging premium. Why has the club structure not displaced syndication entirely? Compare the intermediation cost of a bond issue and a syndicated loan for the same project. Which is cheaper, and does cheaper mean better? C 32

title: Fees: what is charged and who actually pays
blockname: Fees: what is charged and who actually pays
notes: The quantitative heart of the week. Do the fee arithmetic on the board using Gatti’s example.
text: Block D Fees: what is charged and who actually pays The fee stack, the worked example, and the empirical evidence on certification. Indicative length 35 minutes 33

title: The fee stack on a syndicated project financing
blockname: Fees: what is charged and who actually pays
notes: Work Gatti’s numerical example through on the board. Students who have seen the arithmetic once never again describe fees as a detail.
text: The fee stack on a syndicated project financing D Gatti, ch. 6.3. 34 Fee Paid to Basis What it is for Advisory fee The financial adviser Fixed, with a success element Judgement and structuring Arranging fee The lead arranger Basis points on the facility Commitment, certification and distribution Underwriting fee The underwriters Basis points on the amount underwritten Bearing the risk that syndication fails Participation fee Participating banks Basis points on their share, tiered by size Inducement to join Agency fee The agent bank Annual, fixed Administering the facility for its life Commitment fee All lenders On undrawn amounts Compensation for holding capital available Legal and technical costs Advisers Time and materials Verification

title: Who pays for certification
blockname: Fees: what is charged and who actually pays
notes: This is the paper the week is built on. The payment mechanism, through fee split rather than direct charge, is what makes it memorable.
text: Who pays for certification $769bn Value of the 4,122 project finance loans arranged between 1991 and 2005 analysed by Gatti, Kleimeier, Megginson and Steffanoni. The paper asks whether certification by a prestigious arranger creates economic value, and finds that it does. Loans arranged by top-tier banks carry lower overall spreads than those arranged by less prestigious institutions. The more surprising finding is about who pays for that certification. It is not the sponsors. It is the banks participating in the syndicate, who allow top-tier arrangers to retain a larger fraction of the upfront arranging fees. That is a precise, quantified account of an intermediation service: the participants are buying assurance from the arranger, and they pay for it by conceding fee share rather than by writing a cheque. D Gatti, S., Kleimeier, S., Megginson, W. and Steffanoni, A. (2013), Financial Management 42(1), 1–40. 35

title: The management fee and carried interest, restated as a question
blockname: Fees: what is charged and who actually pays
notes: Do the fee drag arithmetic here, as promised in week 3. An eight per cent gross return, a one and a half per cent fee and twenty per cent carry over a hurdle is a very different net number, and the forced exit costs more than the fee.
text: The management fee and carried interest, restated as a question An infrastructure fund charges a management fee on committed or invested capital and takes a share of profits above a hurdle. Over a ten-year fund life on a large commitment, the aggregate is a substantial fraction of the gross return. The question is not whether that is a lot of money. It is what the four frictions from block A say about it. A general partner performs search, because it sources transactions the investor could not. It performs verification, because it diligences them. It performs coordination, because it assembles consortia. Whether those services are worth the fee is an empirical question and the answer plainly varies by manager. What is not defensible is treating the fee as the price of access and declining to ask what it buys. D RE02 Lent lecture 6, leverage, fees and performance; Andonov and others (2021). 36

title: A worked fee example, in outline
blockname: Fees: what is charged and who actually pays
notes: The point of the exhibit is the total, which students consistently underestimate. Nearly three per cent of the facility is consumed before construction begins, and on a large transaction that is a very large number.
text: A worked fee example, in outline D Structure follows Gatti, ch. 6.3. Amounts are illustrative and in millions of a notional currency; work the real example from the text on the board. 37 Item Basis Illustrative amount Facility Senior debt raised 500 Arranging fee 100 basis points on the facility 5.0 Underwriting fee 35 basis points on the underwritten amount 1.75 Participation fees Tiered, 20 to 40 basis points on takes 1.4 Financial advisory Fixed plus success element 2.5 Legal, technical, insurance, model audit Time and materials 4.0 Total As a percentage of the facility About 2.9 per cent

title: How fees are actually negotiated
blockname: Fees: what is charged and who actually pays
notes: The last sentence connects to the relationship intermediation slide in block A and closes a loop students will notice.
text: How fees are actually negotiated Very little of the fee stack is posted. Arranging and underwriting fees are negotiated against market conditions and the borrower’s alternatives, participation fees are set to clear the syndication, and advisory fees are set by competition among a small number of firms who know each other’s pricing. The borrower’s leverage comes from having a credible alternative, which in practice means running a competitive process for the mandate rather than appointing the bank that brought the idea. Sponsors who do this routinely pay materially less, and the reason more do not is that the bank which brought the idea expects the mandate and will not bring the next one if it does not receive it. That is a relationship intermediation equilibrium and it is expensive. D 38

title: The public side pays fees too, and discloses them differently
blockname: Fees: what is charged and who actually pays
notes: Flag this as a dissertation topic. It is genuinely under-researched and the data exist in national audit office reports.
text: The public side pays fees too, and discloses them differently An authority procuring a transaction pays its own advisers, and it also pays the private side’s bid costs indirectly through the price it accepts. Neither is usually reported as a cost of the project. Transparency here is worse than on the private side, because a private sponsor at least knows what it paid. Public reporting typically discloses the capital cost of the asset and not the transaction cost of procuring it, which means the total cost of the intermediation this week describes is not systematically observable anywhere. That is a legitimate research question and it would make a good dissertation. D Delmon, ch. 7.5 and ch. 8.11. 39

title: Block D discussion
blockname: Fees: what is charged and who actually pays
notes: Question two is the arithmetic exercise. Question three is the one that connects to the rating agency debate in block E.
text: Block D discussion Seminar questions Gatti and colleagues find that syndicate participants pay for arranger certification through the fee split. Why would a participant pay rather than doing its own diligence? Compute the difference between gross and net return for a fund charging one and a half per cent on invested capital and twenty per cent above an eight per cent hurdle, over a ten-year life. What has to be true for that to be worth paying? If certification is worth basis points, should the certifier be liable when the certification proves wrong? D 40

title: Does the intermediary add value
notes: The best block in the week. Three clean empirical designs, three different answers, and a real synthesis at the end.
text: Block E Does the intermediary add value Three tests from three markets, and what they agree and disagree about. Indicative length 40 minutes 41

title: A natural experiment on brokerage
notes: The best single teaching paper in the module. It is in a market every student understands and it produces a nuanced answer rather than a verdict.
text: A natural experiment on brokerage AER 2009 Hendel, Nevo and Ortalo-Magné compare house sales made through a broker with sales made without one, in the same city over the same period. The design is unusually clean. An active for-sale-by-owner platform operated alongside the conventional multiple listing service in the same city, so comparable houses could be sold either way. Prices achieved without a broker were no lower than those achieved through the listing service. But selling without a broker took longer and was less likely to result in a sale at all, and patient sellers sorted into the unbrokered channel while patient buyers transacted on the brokered one. The intermediary, on this evidence, is not selling a higher price. It is selling speed and certainty of execution, which are worth a great deal to some sellers and nothing to others. E Hendel, I., Nevo, A. and Ortalo-Magné, F. (2009), American Economic Review 99(5), 1878–1898. 42

title: When adviser quality is worth paying for
notes: The condition is what to put to the guests: is infrastructure a market where reputation is exposed and the task is hard, or is it not.
text: When adviser quality is worth paying for Only sometimes Golubov, Petmezas and Travlos on the value of top-tier financial advisers in mergers and acquisitions. Contrary to earlier studies, they find that top-tier advisers deliver higher returns to bidders, but only in public acquisitions, where the adviser’s reputational exposure and the skills required are greatest. In private deals the effect disappears. The improvement comes from two sources: top-tier advisers identify combinations with greater synergies, and they capture a larger share of those synergies for their client. The conditional result is the interesting one. Adviser quality pays where reputation is on the line and the task is hard, and does not where the transaction is simple or the scrutiny is low. That is a testable proposition about any advisory market, including infrastructure. E Golubov, A., Petmezas, D. and Travlos, N. G. (2012), The Journal of Finance 67(1), 271–311. 43

title: The third test, from the practitioners themselves
notes: This is the sceptical counterweight and it is qualitative evidence, which is worth flagging as a methodological point for the RM01 connection.
text: The third test, from the practitioners themselves Demirag, Khadaroo, Stapleton and Stevenson interviewed the equity and senior debt providers financing private finance projects in the United Kingdom, and recorded how they perceived and priced risk. What emerges is a picture of intermediation that the theoretical literature does not capture: financiers relying heavily on the assurance produced by other parties in the chain, a widespread assumption that somebody else has checked, and risk perceptions shaped by the structure of the network rather than by independent analysis. It is a useful corrective. Certification chains can propagate confidence as easily as information, and a market in which everyone is relying on everyone else’s diligence is more fragile than its documentation suggests. E Demirag, I., Khadaroo, I., Stapleton, P. and Stevenson, C. (2011), The British Accounting Review 43(4), 294–310. 44

title: Three tests, three answers
notes: Build this table at the end of the block. The three quantitative studies agree that intermediaries do something real and disagree about what; the qualitative study warns that the chain may be thinner than it looks.
text: Three tests, three answers E 45 Study Market Design Finding Hendel and others (2009) Residential property Two channels, same market and period The broker sells speed and certainty, not price Golubov and others (2012) Mergers and acquisitions Cross-section by adviser tier and deal type Quality pays where reputation is exposed, not otherwise Gatti and others (2013) Project finance loans 4,122 loans, spreads and fee splits Certification lowers spreads, and participants pay for it Demirag and others (2011) United Kingdom private finance Interviews with financiers Assurance is relied upon more than it is independently verified

title: What the evidence supports, stated carefully
notes: This is the conclusion the block exists to reach and it is a genuine finding rather than a summary. It should be stated with conviction and it should make the guests want to argue.
text: What the evidence supports, stated carefully Intermediaries in these markets are not selling a better price. They are selling execution, certification and access, and those are worth paying for under identifiable conditions: where the task is hard, where reputation is genuinely exposed, and where the alternative is that each party verifies separately at greater total cost. Where those conditions do not hold, the fee is closer to a toll on access. The uncomfortable implication for infrastructure is that the conditions hold most strongly for arranging, where the evidence is clearest, and least strongly for the fund management layer, where the fees are largest and the evidence is thinnest. E 46

title: Selection or treatment
notes: This is the methodological core of the block and the reason the RM01 link is universal this week. Ask students which design they find most convincing before you tell them.
text: Selection or treatment Every study in this block faces the same threat. Better transactions may choose better intermediaries, in which case the observed association between adviser quality and outcome reflects who was hired rather than what they did. The designs differ in how well they handle it. Hendel and colleagues come closest to a solution, because the two channels operate in one market and the sorting itself is observable and modelled. Golubov and colleagues address it through the conditional structure of the result, since a pure selection story struggles to explain why the effect appears in public deals and not in private ones. Gatti and colleagues rely on a large sample and on the fee split, which is hard to explain by selection at all. E RM01 lecture 5, omitted variable bias; RM02 topic 6, experiments and quasi-experiments. 47

title: What would settle the question for infrastructure
notes: The last bullet is honest and it also identifies a genuine research opportunity for a student with access to loan-level data.
text: What would settle the question for infrastructure A setting where comparable assets are transacted with and without an intermediary, which club deals against syndicated deals come closest to providing. An observable outcome that is not itself chosen by the intermediary, since spreads and fees are both negotiated by the party being evaluated. A long enough horizon to see whether the certified transactions performed better, which requires linking origination data to subsequent default data. A source of variation in intermediary presence that is unrelated to deal quality, such as a regulatory change or a bank exit from a market. None of these exists in a usable form for infrastructure at present, which is why the week borrows its evidence from adjacent markets. That is a limitation to state rather than to hide. E 48

title: Block E discussion
text: Block E discussion Seminar questions Hendel and colleagues find that brokers sell speed rather than price. Does that finding transfer to infrastructure transactions, and what would you look for to test it? Golubov and colleagues find adviser quality pays only where reputation is exposed. Is infrastructure such a market? If assurance is relied on more than it is verified, as Demirag and colleagues suggest, where in an infrastructure transaction is the chain weakest? E 49

title: The transaction process end to end
blockname: The transaction process end to end
notes: This block anchors the abstract material in a sequence students can follow, and it repeats the procurement material from week 4 from the intermediary’s side.
text: Block F The transaction process end to end Market sounding, competition, negotiation, and where value is created or lost. Indicative length 30 minutes 50

title: The process, and who is doing what
blockname: The transaction process end to end
notes: Note that the syndication row often happens after financial close, which means the arranger has already committed and is exposed to market movement in the interval. That exposure is what the arranging fee compensates.
text: The process, and who is doing what F Delmon, ch. 8; Gatti, ch. 6.1. 51 Stage What happens Who leads Preparation Feasibility, structuring, documents, approvals Transaction advisers to the authority Market sounding Testing appetite before the documents are fixed Financial adviser, informally Prequalification Screening consortia for capability and capacity The authority, on advice Bidding Consortia assemble, price and submit Sponsors, with their own advisers and lenders Evaluation and preferred bidder Selection, and the beginning of the difficult part The authority Negotiation to close Conditions precedent, final credit approvals, execution Everybody at once Syndication Distribution of the arranged debt The arranger, after close or in parallel

title: Market sounding is the cheapest thing an authority can do
blockname: The transaction process end to end
notes: The second reason is the real one and it connects to the appraisal material in week 2. Announcement before preparation forecloses the useful questions.
text: Market sounding is the cheapest thing an authority can do Before the documents are fixed, an adviser asks the market what it would bid for: which risks it will take, at what price, what would make it decline, and whether the timetable is credible. It costs very little and it prevents the most common procurement failure, which is launching a process the market will not bid for. It is skipped for two reasons, both bad. Officials fear that talking to the market before a tender compromises fairness, which it does not if it is done openly and with all participants. And a project that has already been announced cannot easily absorb the answer that nobody will bid for it. F Delmon, ch. 8.3. 52

title: Where competition ends and negotiation begins
blockname: The transaction process end to end
notes: The last sentence is the transferable insight and it applies to almost any procurement.
text: Where competition ends and negotiation begins The moment a preferred bidder is appointed, the competition ends and a bilateral negotiation begins with a party that knows it. Everything not settled at that point is settled without competitive pressure, and the empirical record of preferred bidder periods is that costs rise and risk allocation moves in one direction. The practical remedies are to settle as much as possible before selection, to keep a reserve bidder credible for as long as possible, and to be willing to return to the market, which authorities almost never are. The intermediation lesson is that the value an adviser adds is concentrated in the design of the process rather than in the negotiation, because by the negotiation stage the leverage has already gone. F Delmon, ch. 8.4; and the renegotiation material from week 2. 53

title: A bidding consortium is a temporary firm
blockname: The transaction process end to end
notes: The temporary firm framing is useful and students find it memorable. It also explains why consortium composition is disclosed and scrutinised at prequalification.
text: A bidding consortium is a temporary firm Four or five organisations with different objectives assemble to bid, spend a year and several million pounds, and dissolve if they lose. They must agree a price, a risk allocation between themselves, and a governance arrangement, all before knowing whether they will win anything. Holding that together is a coordination service in the strict sense, and it is usually performed by the lead sponsor or its financial adviser. It is also where consortia most often fail: not on the bid economics but on the internal agreement, and particularly on what happens if one member wants to leave. The shareholders agreement students met in week 4 is the residue of that negotiation. F Delmon, ch. 19; Gatti, ch. 1.3. 54

title: Exclusivity, and what it costs the party that grants it
blockname: The transaction process end to end
notes: The parallel with preferred bidder appointment is exact and worth drawing. It is the same mistake at a different scale.
text: Exclusivity, and what it costs the party that grants it An adviser or arranger will often ask for exclusivity: a period in which the client may not approach anyone else. The justification is that the work is substantial and speculative, and the adviser will not do it if the client can shop the output. The cost is that the client gives up its only real source of pricing discipline. The reasonable compromise is a short exclusivity for a defined scope, with pricing agreed before it begins, and a clear right to go elsewhere afterwards. Where exclusivity is open-ended and pricing is settled later, the client has agreed to negotiate a fee with a counterparty it cannot leave, which is the position week 2 described a state being in after a preferred bidder is appointed. F 55

title: Block F discussion
blockname: The transaction process end to end
text: Block F discussion Seminar questions Why do authorities so rarely return to the market when a preferred bidder’s price rises? Where in the process would you spend an extra hundred thousand pounds of advisory budget, and why there? The arranger is exposed between commitment and syndication. Should the borrower pay for that exposure, or should the arranger not take it? F 56

title: Principal against intermediary
notes: The guest hour, and the reason this week is structured as it is. Set up the question before they speak.
text: Block G Principal against intermediary A fund manager and a permanent capital investor, on what intermediation is worth. Indicative length 30 minutes 57

title: The question the guests embody
notes: Say this before they arrive. It gives students a frame and it gives the guests permission to disagree, which is what makes the session worth an hour.
text: The question the guests embody One of this week’s guests is an intermediary in the strict sense: a general partner standing between limited partner capital and the underlying assets, sourcing transactions, and charging a fee and a share of profits for doing it. The other is a principal with permanent capital, buying directly and holding indefinitely, with no fund life and no external investors to answer to. They are not simply two practitioners from the same industry. They occupy opposite positions on the question the week has been asking, and the useful hour is the one in which that disagreement is made explicit rather than smoothed over. G 58

title: The two positions
notes: Give both columns before the guests speak, so students can test what they hear against a stated position rather than being persuaded by whoever is more articulate.
text: The two positions The intermediary’s case Access. Transactions are sourced through relationships an investor cannot replicate at any reasonable cost Capability. An underwriting and asset management team is expensive and only justified at scale Diversification. A fund gives exposure to twelve assets where direct investment gives one Governance. Somebody has to sit on the board and manage the asset, and most investors cannot The fee is the price of all of that, and the alternative is not participating The principal’s case The fee compounds. Over a thirty-year hold it is the largest single deduction from return The fund life forces a sale at a date chosen by the calendar rather than by the market Alignment. A manager is paid on deployment and exit, not on holding a good asset well Information. The owner who runs the asset knows things a limited partner never will Permanent capital can do what a fund cannot, which is wait G 59

title: Questions to put to the guests
notes: The last question closes the week on the block A framework and is the one to keep if time is short.
text: Questions to put to the guests What proportion of the transactions you complete could the investor have found without you? Be specific. For the principal: what have you given up by not using managers, and when have you regretted it? For the manager: what would you charge if the fund had no fixed life, and would the model still work? Both: name a transaction that only happened because an intermediary made it happen, and one that was worse for having them. Both: which of the four frictions, search, information, verification or coordination, is the one you are actually paid to solve? G 60

title: Block G discussion
text: Block G discussion Seminar questions After hearing both, which of the four frictions is the fund manager actually removing, and is the fee proportionate to it? A permanent capital investor can wait. What is the option value of being able to wait, and how would you estimate it? If the evidence says intermediaries sell execution and certification rather than price, which of this week’s guests is selling which? G 61

title: Reserve material
notes: Not part of the two-hour session.
text: Block H Reserve material Slides held back from the main sequence. Indicative length As required 62

title: The gap this week does not fill
notes: An honest statement of a known gap. Better to say it than to have students discover it.
text: The gap this week does not fill The syllabus lists valuation among the topics for this week, meaning valuation in the transaction sense: what an asset is worth in a sale rather than what a project’s cash flows discount to. Neither the set texts nor the journal articles treat it, and the module reading list records the gap honestly. Week 6 supplies project appraisal, which is a different thing. What is missing is the pricing of an operating asset in a bilateral negotiation, where comparables are scarce, the buyer and seller have different costs of capital, and much of the value turns on what each believes about the regulatory settlement after next. That material should come from the guests or be written before the module runs a second time. H 63

title: Candidate cases for Week 5
notes: The club deal against the syndicated deal is the strongest comparison and the closest thing to a controlled experiment the market offers.
text: Candidate cases for Week 5 H 64 Case What it illustrates Material A large syndicated project financing Arranging, underwriting, fee split and distribution League tables and public deal reporting A club deal for the same kind of asset The market’s own test of the arranging premium Bank disclosures and trade press A continuation vehicle The manager selling to itself, and the conflicts in it Secondary market commentary A refinancing into the bond market The same functions performed by different intermediaries Prospectuses are public An unsolicited proposal A transaction with no competition and one adviser National audit reports

title: Sources drawn on for this deck
notes: Keep in the student-facing version.
text: Sources drawn on for this deck Gatti, S. (2024), Project Finance in Theory and Practice, chapters 4, 6 and 7. Delmon, J., Private Sector Investment in Infrastructure, chapters 7, 8 and 11. Flyvbjerg, B. (ed.) (2017), The Oxford Handbook of Megaproject Management, chapter 11. Abor, J. Y. and others (eds) (2025), The Routledge Handbook of Infrastructure Finance, chapter 12. Journal articles as cited on each slide. H 65

title: Where Week 5 leaves us
notes: Four sentences. The last one is the week’s argument and it should be delivered as such.
text: Where Week 5 leaves us An intermediary earns its fee by removing search, information, verification or coordination costs, and any fee not attached to one of those is a toll. Certification is real and priced: prestigious arrangers lower spreads, and the syndicate rather than the sponsor pays for it. The best evidence from adjacent markets says intermediaries sell execution and certainty rather than a better price. The conditions under which intermediation is worth paying for hold most strongly where the evidence is clearest, and least strongly where the fees are largest. 66
